Switching to a cheaper fund in a taxable account: tax now versus fees later

Selling a fund with a gain in a non-registered account triggers capital gains tax. This guide shows when a lower fee pays that back, why a small fee saving on a large gain may never catch up, and why the same switch inside an RRSP or TFSA is tax-free. Four charts and an editable calculator.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 3 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Original illustration for a non-registered account. Switching is treated as a sale: the taxable part of the gain is taxed now and paid from the proceeds, and the rest is invested in the cheaper fund with a new cost base. Both funds earn the same return before fees and are sold at the end, when remaining gains are taxed at the same rate. Annual fund distributions, losses, deferred sales charges, foreign tax and changes in your tax rate are not modelled. Registered accounts (RRSP, TFSA, RRIF) have no capital gains tax on a switch. Confirm with a tax professional whether a particular switch is a disposition.

The central idea

Most of the tax on a switch is tax you would pay eventually anyway; what you really lose is the growth on the money paid early. A one-point fee saving usually wins quickly, but a quarter-point saving on a large gain may never catch up.

01

Why switching can cost tax

In a non-registered (taxable) account, selling one fund to buy another is usually a disposition. If the fund is worth more than your adjusted cost base—roughly what you paid plus reinvested distributions—you have a capital gain. Only part of a gain is taxable: CRA's capital gains guide uses an inclusion rate of one-half, so half the gain is added to your income and taxed at your marginal rate. Switches inside an RRSP, RRIF, TFSA or FHSA do not create capital gains tax.

The model starts with a fund worth CAD 100,000 with a cost base of CAD 70,000, a 40% marginal tax rate and a one-half inclusion rate. Switching today triggers CAD 6,000 of tax (CAD 30,000 gain × ½ × 40%), paid from the proceeds, so CAD 94,000 goes into the new fund.

02

Most of that tax is timing, not extra cost

If you keep the old fund, the same gain is still taxed when you eventually sell—or at death. A fair comparison therefore looks at what you would have after tax if you sold everything in a given year, under both choices. In the model both funds earn 6% before fees; the current fund costs 2.2% a year and the new one 1.2%.

If you sold in year 15, keeping the old fund would leave about CAD 153,975 after tax and switching about CAD 170,728—CAD 16,753 more. With a full point of fee saving, switching is ahead from the first year. The tax paid today is mostly tax brought forward; the cost is only the growth those CAD 6,000 would have earned.

03

When switching does not pay

The picture changes when the gain is large and the fee saving small. With a cost base of only CAD 20,000, switching triggers CAD 16,000 of tax. A 0.5-point saving then takes about 20 years to break even, and a 0.25-point saving never catches up in 60 years: the lost growth on the tax paid early outweighs the fee saved each year. The break-even chart shows how quickly the answer flips as the fee gap narrows.

Other points to check: whether a change between series of the same fund counts as a disposition for your account; whether the old fund still carries deferred sales charges; whether you can switch gradually across tax years or use capital losses elsewhere; and whether moving the money into a TFSA or RRSP with available room fits your plan.

04

What the model leaves out

Funds in taxable accounts also pay yearly distributions that are taxed as you go; both funds are assumed to have the same distributions, so they are left out. The model does not include capital losses, provincial differences in your tax rate, changes in your tax bracket on the sale, foreign withholding tax or the timing of tax instalments. It is an illustration to frame a conversation with your advisor and tax professional, not a filing calculation.
